summary.text: After factoring out the initial power of \(b\), introduce carries in \(\{0,-1\}\); the four possible sign/carry combinations produce ordinary digits only in \(\{0,1,b-2,b-1\}\), and the resulting identity telescopes. If the terminal carry is \(-1\), use \(b^m-V=1+\overline V\): digitwise base-\(b\) complementation preserves the allowed set, while the added \(1\) changes only the least significant digit to another allowed value.

full_proof.text:
Let \(b\ge 5\), let \(n\ge 0\), and choose signs \(\sigma_k\in\{-1,1\}\) for \(1\le k\le n\). Put
\[
X=\sum_{k=1}^n \sigma_k b^k.
\]
We prove that every digit in the ordinary base-\(b\) expansion of \(|X|\) belongs to
\[
A_b:=\{0,1,b-2,b-1\}.
\]

We will regard finite digit strings as being written from least significant digit to most significant digit. Thus, for a list
\[
L=(\ell_0,\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_{m-1})
\]
of nonnegative integers, define
\[
\operatorname{val}_b(L)=\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}\ell_jb^j.
\]
We first record three elementary facts about such lists.

**Fact 1 (reading a valid digit list).** If every entry of \(L\) is less than \(b\), then every digit in the ordinary base-\(b\) expansion of \(\operatorname{val}_b(L)\) is either an entry of \(L\) or \(0\).

Indeed, this follows by induction on the length of \(L\). For the empty list the value is \(0\), so there is nothing to prove (and under a convention that displays zero with one digit, that digit is \(0\)). If \(L=(h,T)\), then
\[
\operatorname{val}_b(L)=h+b\operatorname{val}_b(T),\qquad 0\le h<b.
\]
If this value is nonzero, its least significant digit is its remainder modulo \(b\), namely \(h\), and the quotient after division by \(b\) is \(\operatorname{val}_b(T)\). The assertion therefore follows from the induction hypothesis for \(T\). If the value is zero, again only the digit \(0\) can occur. This also explains why the harmless extra alternative \(0\) is included: high-order zero entries in a list are normally omitted from the standard expansion.

**Fact 2 (size bound).** If \(L\) has length \(m\) and all its entries are less than \(b\), where \(b>1\), then
\[
\operatorname{val}_b(L)<b^m.
\]
This is immediate either from
\[
\operatorname{val}_b(L)\le (b-1)(1+b+\cdots+b^{m-1})=b^m-1,
\]
or by induction on the length.

**Fact 3 (base complement).** Under the same hypotheses,
\[
b^m-\operatorname{val}_b(L)
 =1+\operatorname{val}_b(\overline L),
\]
where \(\overline L\) is obtained by replacing every entry \(\ell_j\) by its base complement \(b-1-\ell_j\). To see this, calculate
\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{val}_b(\overline L)
 &=\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}(b-1-\ell_j)b^j\\
 &=(b-1)\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}b^j-\operatorname{val}_b(L)\\
 &=b^m-1-\operatorname{val}_b(L).
\end{aligned}
\]
The size bound ensures that all subtractions here have their usual nonnegative interpretation.

We now convert the signed powers into ordinary digits by an explicit borrow construction.

If \(n=0\), then \(X=0\), and the assertion is immediate. Hence suppose \(n\ge 1\). Factor out one power of \(b\), and reindex the signs by setting
\[
\tau_j=\sigma_{j+1}\qquad(0\le j<n).
\]
Extend \(\tau_j\) to all \(j\ge 0\), for example by setting \(\tau_j=1\) when \(j\ge n\). Thus every \(\tau_j\) is still either \(1\) or \(-1\), and
\[
X=bS,
\qquad
S:=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\tau_jb^j.
\]

Define a sequence of borrows \(c_j\) by
\[
c_0=0,
\qquad
c_{j+1}=
\begin{cases}
0,&\tau_j=1,\\
-1,&\tau_j=-1.
\end{cases}
\]
Thus every \(c_j\) is either \(0\) or \(-1\). Define
\[
d_j=\tau_j+c_j-bc_{j+1}.
\]
We claim that every \(d_j\) is an ordinary base-\(b\) digit belonging to \(A_b\). There are two cases according to \(\tau_j\).

If \(\tau_j=1\), then \(c_{j+1}=0\), and hence
\[
d_j=1+c_j.
\]
Since \(c_j\in\{0,-1\}\), this gives \(d_j\in\{1,0\}\).

If \(\tau_j=-1\), then \(c_{j+1}=-1\), and hence
\[
d_j=-1+c_j+b=b-1+c_j.
\]
Thus \(d_j\in\{b-1,b-2\}\).

Consequently
\[
d_j\in\{0,1,b-2,b-1\}=A_b
\]
for every \(j\). Because \(b\ge5\), all four possibilities are nonnegative and strictly less than \(b\), so they are valid base-\(b\) digits.

The definition of \(d_j\) can be rearranged as
\[
\tau_j=d_j-c_j+bc_{j+1}.
\]
Multiplying by \(b^j\) and summing from \(j=0\) to \(n-1\), we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
S
&=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}d_jb^j
  -\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}c_jb^j
  +\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}c_{j+1}b^{j+1}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The last two sums telescope: after shifting the index in the last sum, all intermediate terms cancel, while \(c_0=0\). Therefore
\[
S=V+c_nb^n,
\qquad
V:=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}d_jb^j.
\]
Equivalently, if
\[
D=(d_0,d_1,\ldots,d_{n-1}),
\]
then \(V=\operatorname{val}_b(D)\), and
\[
X=b\bigl(V+c_nb^n\bigr).
\]
Since \(c_n\) is either \(0\) or \(-1\), there are two cases.

### Case 1: \(c_n=0\)

Then
\[
X=bV\ge0,
\qquad |X|=bV.
\]
Every entry of \(D\) is a member of \(A_b\) and is less than \(b\). By Fact 1, every digit of \(V=\operatorname{val}_b(D)\) is therefore in \(A_b\) (the possible extra digit \(0\) is already in \(A_b\)). Multiplication by \(b\) merely shifts a base-\(b\) expansion one place to the left and inserts a least significant zero, unless \(V=0\), in which case the result is zero. Hence every digit of \(|X|=bV\) lies in \(A_b\).

### Case 2: \(c_n=-1\)

Now
\[
X=b(V-b^n).
\]
The list \(D\) has length \(n\), and all its entries are less than \(b\). Fact 2 gives
\[
V<b^n.
\]
Thus \(X<0\), and
\[
|X|=b(b^n-V).
\]
By Fact 3,
\[
b^n-V
 =1+\operatorname{val}_b(b-1-d_0,\,b-1-d_1,\ldots,b-1-d_{n-1}).
\]
The addition of \(1\) can be absorbed into the least significant entry. Explicitly,
\[
1+\operatorname{val}_b(b-1-d_0,\,b-1-d_1,\ldots,b-1-d_{n-1})
=
\operatorname{val}_b(F),
\]
where
\[
F=(b-d_0,\,b-1-d_1,\ldots,b-1-d_{n-1}).
\]
We must check that the entries of \(F\) are valid digits and all belong to \(A_b\).

For every \(j\ge1\), we already know that \(d_j\in A_b\). Complementation by \(x\mapsto b-1-x\) preserves \(A_b\), because it interchanges the four digits in pairs:
\[
0\longleftrightarrow b-1,

eqquad
1\longleftrightarrow b-2.
\]
Therefore
\[
b-1-d_j\in A_b\qquad(1\le j<n).
\]

The least significant entry requires the slight modification \(b-d_0\), rather than \(b-1-d_0\), because of the added \(1\). Here the initial condition \(c_0=0\) gives a sharper description of \(d_0\). If \(\tau_0=1\), then \(c_1=0\) and
\[
d_0=1+c_0=1,
\]
so \(b-d_0=b-1\). If \(\tau_0=-1\), then \(c_1=-1\) and
\[
d_0=-1+c_0+b=b-1,
\]
so \(b-d_0=1\). Thus the first entry of \(F\) is either \(1\) or \(b-1\), and in particular is also in \(A_b\) and is less than \(b\).

It follows that every entry of \(F\) lies in \(A_b\) and is a valid base-\(b\) digit. Since
\[
b^n-V=\operatorname{val}_b(F),
\]
Fact 1 shows that every ordinary base-\(b\) digit of \(b^n-V\) lies in \(A_b\). Finally, multiplication by \(b\) only appends a least significant zero. Therefore every digit of
\[
|X|=b\operatorname{val}_b(F)
\]
also lies in \(A_b\).

The two cases exhaust the possible terminal borrow \(c_n\), proving the claim for every assignment of signs. In particular, taking \(\sigma_k=-1\) when \(k\) is prime and \(\sigma_k=1\) otherwise gives the partial sums defining A243106 (with \(b=10\)); their absolute values therefore use only the digits \(0,1,8,9\). More generally, in every base \(b>4\), every independently signed sum of the first \(n\) positive powers of \(b\) has absolute value whose base-\(b\) digits all belong to \(\{0,1,b-2,b-1\}\).
